title: All Dilute Gases Behave Ideally
lead: Particles of an ideal gas exert no forces on each other, only on the walls they strike. Their collisions with the walls lead to the ideal gas law, an equation of state, and the compressibility factor measures how far a real gas strays from it.
notes: Adapted from Mark Tuckerman (New York University) and Jerry LaRue (Chapman University); Figure 16.1.2 is from OpenStax Chemistry under CC BY. Figure 16.3.1, the ideal isotherms of one mole, is folded into Figure 16.1.1, and a broken duplicate of the page's thumbnail is left out.
exercise_notes: The book prints no exercises for this section; both questions and their solutions were written by AI, the numbers computed with k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and an N₂ molecule of 4.652 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: (Left) Pressure vs. volume for different temperatures (isotherms of the ideal-gas equation of state. (Right) Pressure vs. temperature for different densities $\rho = N/V$. Ideal gas isotherms for one mole of the gas and at select temperatures. (public domain).
A graph of the compressibility factor (Z) vs. pressure shows that gases can exhibit significant deviations from the behavior predicted by the ideal gas law. from Openstax (CC-BY)

exercises.prompt: A 1.00 L box holds 0.0100 mol of N₂ at 300 K; one molecule has a mass of $4.652\times10^{-26}$ kg. Find (a) $\langle\kvx^2\rangle$, (b) the pressure from $\kP = N\km\langle\kvx^2\rangle/\kV$, and (c) the pressure from $\kP = \knmol\kR\kT/\kV$. ($k_B = 1.381\times10^{-23}$ J/K, $N_0 = 6.022\times10^{23}$ mol⁻¹, $\kR = 8.314$ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.)

answer.solution: (a) $\langle\kvx^2\rangle = k_B\kT/\km = (1.381\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K})(300\ \text{K})/(4.652\times10^{-26}\ \text{kg}) = 8.906\times10^{4}$ m²/s². (b) There are $N = (0.0100)(6.022\times10^{23}) = 6.022\times10^{21}$ molecules, so $\kP = (6.022\times10^{21})(4.652\times10^{-26}\ \text{kg})(8.906\times10^{4}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2)/(1.00\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3) = 2.49\times10^{4}$ Pa. (c) $\kP = (0.0100\ \text{mol})(8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1})(300\ \text{K})/(1.00\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3) = 2.49\times10^{4}$ Pa. The two agree because $N\km\langle\kvx^2\rangle = Nk_B\kT = \knmol\kR\kT$.

exercises.prompt: A sample of gas is doubled in size with $N/\kV$ held constant. Which list holds only quantities that stay the same?

answer.hint: An intensive property is unchanged when the system grows at constant $N/\kV$.
answer.solution: $\kP$, $\kT$, $\krho$ and $\kVbar$ are intensive. $\krho = N/\kV$ is the ratio held fixed, and $\kVbar = \kV/\knmol$ is a ratio of two quantities that both double, so neither changes. $N$, $\knmol$, $\kV$ and $\km$ double with the sample, so they are extensive.

footnotes.html: $Z$ is the compressibility factor, the name Figure 16.1.2 and Sections 16.3 and 16.4 use. The compressibility of a gas is a different quantity.

With $\rho = N/V$ a number of particles per volume, the last line of Equation 16.1.11 reads $P = \rho k_BT$, and the last form of $Z$ reads $P/\rho k_BT$; $P = \rho RT$ holds for $\rho = n/V$ in moles per volume. Only the first line, $PV = nRT$, is in extensive quantities; the other two are intensive.
The book's image labels the vertical axis Z (kPa); $Z = PV/nRT$ has no unit.

derivations.what: the ideal gas law from wall collisions
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 16.1 All Dilute Gases Behave Ideally

assumes.text: In an elastic collision, all that happens to the velocity is that it changes sign. Thus, if $\kvx$ is the velocity in the $x$ direction before the collision, then $-\kvx$ is the velocity after, and $\kdvx = -\kvx - \kvx = -2\kvx$.

then.why: According to Newton’s second law, the force $-\kFx$ on the particle in this direction gives rise to an acceleration, $a_x = \kdvx/\kdt$, where $\kdt$ is the time interval between collisions with the same wall of the box.

assumes.text: The particles move at constant speed, since no forces act on them except when they collide with the wall. The total distance in the $x$ direction traversed is $2\ka$, and since the speed in the $x$ direction is always $\kvx$, the interval $\kdt = \dfrac{2\ka}{\kvx}$.
The particle pushes on the wall with $\kFx$ and the wall pushes back with $-\kFx$.

$\langle \kF \rangle$ is the average force exerted by all $N$ particles on a wall of the box of area $\kA$; on the wall at $x = 0$ it is $N\langle\kFx\rangle$, because we have $N$ particles hitting the wall.

steps.cap: Averaging $\kFx = \km\kvx^2/\ka$ over the particles averages only $\kvx^2$, since $\km$ and $\ka$ are the same for every one.
